question: How does a UN decision get made, paid for and carried out, and who controls each step?
answer: A General Assembly decision passes through 13 steps, each with its own controller: Member States authorize; a state, organ or the Secretary-General asks for an agenda item; the General Committee filters it; a Main Committee takes the work; sponsors and co-facilitators write the text; the Assembly adopts it (two thirds for budget and other important questions, a simple majority otherwise); then the Fifth Committee and ACABQ decide the money, the Secretary-General carries it out, and auditors and Member States review it. Adoption is not funding, and funding is not delivery.

sections.title: The short version: seven steps
sections.sub: The UN chart's summary of how any UN body acts.

Member States, presidents/chairs, secretariats and rules

Sponsors, facilitators, committees and secretariat drafters

Competent intergovernmental organ

GA/Fifth Committee, agency conference/board, donors or shareholders
Assessment, appropriation, voluntary grant, quota or capital allocation
A mandate without money may remain only partially executable.
Secretary-General, executive head, mission, fund/programme or agency secretariat
Staffing, procurement, country programme, mission or platform
Execution is bounded by delegated authority and host/partner agreements.
Auditors, oversight bodies, legislative reviews and governing boards
Audit, evaluation, compliance finding, performance report or renewed mandate
Findings must re-enter an authority and budget route to change the system.

sections.title: The full chain: 13 steps in the General Assembly
sections.sub: Who controls each step, the record it leaves, and the informal leverage around it.

items.title: Step 1: Authority source
kv: Who controls it
Member States acting through the General Assembly or another competent intergovernmental organ
The record it leaves
Charter article, resolution, decision, terms of reference or organ mandate
What it is not
Political attention, a speech or a side event is not by itself a formal mandate.
What happens

A Charter power, prior resolution, decision or organ mandate creates the legal-political basis for work. A Secretary-General initiative can propose or organize activity within existing authority but does not substitute for Member-State authorization where a new mandate is required.
Informal leverage
The actor that defines the initial problem can make later options appear natural or out of scope.

sources.label: UN work plan and system structure

items.title: Step 2: Agenda inscription
kv: Who controls it
A Member State, principal organ or the Secretary-General may request an item; the Secretary-General compiles the provisional agenda
The record it leaves
Provisional agenda, supplementary list, request letter and explanatory memorandum
What it is not
Placement on a provisional list is not final inclusion or substantive agreement.
What happens

A proposed item is attached to an agenda title. Under the rules, it should carry an explanatory memorandum and, where possible, basic documents or a draft resolution. Timing determines whether it is provisional, supplementary or an urgent additional item.
Informal leverage
The agenda title and explanatory memorandum define the first official description of the problem.

sources.label: A/520/Rev.21 — Rules of Procedure of the General Assembly

items.title: Step 3: Inclusion and priority gate
kv: Who controls it
General Committee recommends; General Assembly approves
The record it leaves
General Committee report and Assembly decision adopting the agenda
What it is not
The General Committee is not supposed to decide the substance while reviewing inclusion.
What happens

The General Committee reviews inclusion, rejection, deferral and priority. The Assembly then approves the agenda and can amend or delete items. This is the formal choke point between proposing a subject and giving it Assembly time.
Informal leverage
PGA leadership, bureau consultations and delegations' willingness to contest inclusion affect whether the item advances smoothly or becomes a procedural fight.

sources.label: General Committee rules and agenda functions

items.title: Step 4: Venue and work-programme routing
kv: Who controls it
General Assembly on General Committee recommendation; then the relevant Main Committee and its bureau
The record it leaves
Allocation decision, committee programme of work and Journal schedule
What it is not
A committee cannot introduce a new agenda item on its own initiative.
What happens

The item is kept in plenary or allocated to one of six Main Committees. The receiving committee adopts priorities, meeting dates and a programme of work. Venue determines which delegates, expertise, precedents and negotiation habits dominate.
Informal leverage
Regional groups influence bureau composition; chairs can group related items, manage time and organize informal negotiations.

items.title: Step 5: Modalities and outcome architecture
kv: Who controls it
Member States through a modalities resolution or decision, often negotiated by appointed co-facilitators
The record it leaves
Modalities resolution, PGA appointment letter, concept note and logistics note
What it is not
A modalities resolution authorizes a process; it does not pre-adopt the eventual declaration.
What happens

The Assembly can specify the meeting date, format, participation, panels, hearings, co-chairs, requested reports and whether a declaration or other outcome is expected. This designs the container before the substantive event occurs.
Informal leverage
Co-facilitators and the PGA shape the options circulated to delegations and the rhythm of consultations.

sources.label: PGA81 meetings, consultations and event documents

items.title: Step 6: Evidence and framing packet
kv: Who controls it
The requesting intergovernmental body controls report mandates; the Secretary-General, Secretariat, expert panels and convenors produce the requested material
The record it leaves
Secretary-General report, concept note, hearing summary, data annex and PGA letter
What it is not
A report is evidence or advice, not a Member-State decision.
What happens
Reports, concept notes, hearing summaries, metrics and background papers define categories, evidence and unresolved questions. The PGA can also set a session theme and priorities after consultation.
Informal leverage
Who selects the evidence base controls vocabulary and the range of claims that appear administratively actionable.

sources.label: PGA81 letters, statements and public record
General Debate theme selection and UNGA81 theme

items.title: Step 7: Access, accreditation and speaking roles
kv: Who controls it
Governments designate state speakers; the PGA, Secretariat or event convenor administers registration and any stakeholder selection under the applicable modalities
The record it leaves
e-Speakers/e-deleGATE registration, participant list, programme and accreditation notice
What it is not
Nationality is not representation; a panel invitation does not confer a state mandate or a vote.
What happens
Speaker lists, panel seats, stakeholder accreditations, moderator roles and public or closed status determine which voices enter the room and in what capacity.
Informal leverage
Invitation, sequencing, moderator questions and keynote status can elevate some perspectives without changing formal voting rights.

items.title: Step 8: Draft ownership and text production
kv: Who controls it
Sponsors, co-sponsors or Member-State co-facilitators own intergovernmental proposals; the Secretariat circulates and services them
The record it leaves
L-document, zero draft, compilation text, Rev.1/Rev.2, co-facilitator letter or silence text
What it is not
Secretariat drafting support and document issuance do not transfer political authorship from Member States.
What happens

A sponsor text or zero draft becomes the negotiating object. Co-facilitators compile written comments, issue revisions and sometimes place compromise language under silence. Delegations control the content of proposals they sponsor.
Informal leverage
The first draft has anchoring power; the drafter decides what must be removed rather than what must be added.

sources.label: General Assembly plenary proposals, procedure and voting
General Assembly drafting and consultation practices
PGA81 letters, statements and public record

items.title: Step 9: Informal negotiation and procedural steering
kv: Who controls it
Member States negotiate; chairs, coordinators and co-facilitators manage the process under authority delegated by the body or PGA
The record it leaves
Programme of consultations, coordinator draft, revised text, silence letter and record of broken or completed silence
What it is not
Closed negotiation can shape the text while leaving a thin public transcript; consensus can coexist with reservations or disassociation.
What happens

Formal debate is followed by informal consultations, smaller drafting groups or informal-informals. Chairs manage speaker lists, deadlines, revisions, points of order and the route to consensus or vote. Silence is a working method, not proof of substantive unanimity.
Informal leverage
Coalitions, regional groups, subject-matter blocs and delegations with drafting capacity often determine which compromises are technically ready for adoption.

sources.label: PGA81 meetings, consultations and event documents
Committee for Programme and Coordination — consensus practice

items.title: Step 10: Decision and adoption
kv: Who controls it
The General Assembly or competent committee/body
The record it leaves
Adopted resolution or decision, meeting record, voting record and explanations of position
What it is not
Adoption creates an authoritative decision or recommendation, not funding, delivery or observed effect.
What happens

The body adopts by consensus or without a vote when no formal objection requires a vote, or it votes under the applicable majority rule. Important questions, including budgetary questions, require two thirds of members present and voting; other questions generally require a simple majority.
Informal leverage
Sponsors decide whether to press for a vote; delegations can seek amendments, division, explanations of vote or recorded reservations.

sources.label: General Assembly plenary proposals, procedure and voting
Committee for Programme and Coordination — consensus practice

items.title: Step 11: Programme and resource authorization
kv: Who controls it
Secretary-General proposes; CPC reviews programme plans; ACABQ examines resources; Fifth Committee negotiates; General Assembly approves
The record it leaves
Programme plan, proposed budget, PBI or revised estimate, CPC report, ACABQ report and Fifth Committee resolution
What it is not
An adopted substantive resolution may remain weakly implemented if resources, posts or voluntary funding do not follow.
What happens

A mandate with expenditure implications must meet the budget process. Programme budget implications or revised estimates translate policy language into posts and money. ACABQ recommendations are the working starting point for Fifth Committee negotiations.
Informal leverage
Resource ceilings, documentation timing and ACABQ recommendations can narrow a mandate without rewriting its political language.

sources.label: Fifth Committee budget process and ACABQ role
ST/SGB/2018/3 — planning, budgeting, monitoring and evaluation

items.title: Step 12: Administrative execution and delivery network
kv: Who controls it

Secretary-General as chief administrative officer, then heads of entity under delegated authority; separately governed UN funds, programmes and specialized agencies act under their own mandates and budgets
The record it leaves
Delegation instrument, programme plan, allotment, procurement, grant or partnership agreement, project document and operating output
What it is not
The UN system is not one command hierarchy; many entities have separate leadership, budgets and governing bodies.
What happens

Approved work is assigned to departments, offices, missions or delivery partners. Managers exercise delegated financial, staffing, procurement and property authority; funds and agencies may need their own governing-body decisions and voluntary finance.
Informal leverage
Implementation control shifts toward whoever holds staff, systems, procurement authority, country presence, technical expertise and partner relationships.

sources.label: UN system entities, mandates and budgets

items.title: Step 13: Record, oversight and renewal
kv: Who controls it
Secretariat records services; programme managers report; Member States and oversight bodies review
The record it leaves
Journal entry, PV/SR record, ODS document, performance report, audit/evaluation and follow-up resolution
What it is not
A polished public record can show process without proving implementation quality or real-world effect.
What happens

DGACM creates the Journal, document trail and meeting records; managers report results; OIOS, the Board of Auditors and JIU test performance and controls; Member States can renew, amend, resource, defer or terminate the mandate in a later cycle.
Informal leverage
Indicators and document architecture determine what becomes visible, comparable and reusable in the next round of agenda setting.

sources.label: DGACM meeting management, Journal and records
ST/SGB/2018/3 — planning, budgeting, monitoring and evaluation

sections.title: The founding documents behind the steps

rows.text: Charter of the United Nations
Creates the principal organs, allocates powers and provides the bridge to specialized agencies.
Statute of the International Court of Justice
Creates the independent judicial body, election mechanism, contentious jurisdiction and advisory function.
Convention on the Privileges and Immunities of the United Nations

rows: UN property, representatives, officials and experts

rows.text: Protects institutional independence, premises, archives, assets and official functions.
UN–U.S. Headquarters Agreement
rows.note: Arts. II–IX; especially access, communications, privileges and dispute settlement

rows.text: Converts the U.S. host role into treaty obligations designed to let the UN function independently.
United Nations Participation Act
Creates the U.S. Mission structure, appointment routes and instruction/voting chain.
General Assembly Rules of Procedure
Turns Charter powers into agenda, committee, voting and budget procedure.
WHO Constitution
Separates Health Assembly, Executive Board and Director-General powers and authorizes specific normative instruments.
UNESCO Constitution
Assigns policy and budget to the General Conference, agenda/execution to the Executive Board and administration to the Director-General.
FAO Constitution and Basic Texts
Creates the Conference, Council, committees and Director-General with their own one-member/one-vote governance.
ITU Constitution and Convention
Defines membership, instruments, Plenipotentiary Conference, Council and General Secretariat.
IMF Articles of Agreement
rows.note: Arts. I–III, V, IX–X, XII–XIII, XXVIII

rows.text: Creates quota resources, weighted voting, Board/Executive structure and special-majority locks.
IBRD Articles of Agreement

rows: International Bank for Reconstruction and Development

rows.text: Creates capital subscriptions, weighted voting, Governors, Executive Directors and Bank legal status.

uncertain: This is a functional legal map, not a claim that every body shown is hierarchically subordinate to the box above it.
These are the rules and the usual route; a given resolution can skip or repeat steps, and the informal leverage column is the package's reading, not a rule.
